edits.fix: Change the footer template on all seven pages to the standard form 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>', with a band-specific page id such as K1-1, instead of a bare right-aligned page number.

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover the top shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a different copy.
edits.fix: Say how each way is kept, e.g. 'Trace around the blocks on each copy', so the found ways stay on the page after the blocks are reused. The two coverings of the small hexagon are turns of each other, so expect K-1 children to call them 'the same'. The adult can settle that a turned covering counts as a new way because the board does not move.

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover this shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a different copy. There are more copies on the next page.
edits.fix: Read literally, this leaves blocks on every copy: 6 ways x 8 rhombi = 48 blue blocks per child or group, plus more blocks on the two spare copies. Ask the children to trace or color each way on its copy so the K-1 group is not short of blue blocks and the six ways survive for the closing share.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 packet that is concrete and correctly drawn at actual size: possible and impossible shapes (including an even-area trapezoid that cannot be covered), fewest greens on triangles of sides 2 to 4 (answers 2, 3, 4), coverings of growing hexagons (2, 3, then 6 ways, with spare copies), fewest mixed blocks (3, 3, 4) and a blue-block placement game (answers 1st, 2nd, 1st, 1st, 2nd). All the answers check out, and six problems give enough work for the hour. The only edits are how children record the coverings in P3 and P6 and the footer id.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' with a band-specific id such as G23-1 on all seven pages.

edits.quote: The board must stay in one piece if you cut it out.
edits.fix: Board F on page 2 joins two triangles at a single point and is treated as one board. Children can therefore argue that corner-touching pieces count, which makes P6 easy: five separate side-2 triangles give 10 greens. Replace the sentence with 'Every small triangle of your board must share a whole edge with another triangle of the board; touching only at a corner, as in board F, does not count.'

grades-2-3.summary: The best-developed band: it builds the up/down coloring obstruction with well-chosen contrasts. In P1 the star is forced and the even-area trapezoid is impossible. P2 contrasts an imbalanced hexagon, a balanced hourglass pinched at a point, and a tileable balanced hexagon. Then come the sharp bound n with its proof (P4), the comparison with chevrons (answers 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5), a design problem that has solutions, and the converse rule on the side-2 hexagon, where all 144 placements of one up and one down triangle work. All the mathematics checks out. Only the corner-touching ambiguity in P6 and the footer need changes.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' with a band-specific id such as G45-1 on all eight pages.

edits.quote: Which two coverings need the most moves to get from one to the other? How many moves do they need?
edits.fix: The ten small boards in P1 (page 1) have no labels, so children cannot name the two coverings in their answer. Put a letter under each small board in P1 and ask in P2 for the letters of the two coverings. The expected answer is the unique pair at distance 4 in the six-covering flip graph.

grades-4-5.summary: A rich and correct development of kernel 2. It moves from all 6 coverings of the (1,2,2) board and the flip move (greatest distance 4) to flip distances on the side-2 hexagon, where the drawn coverings are valid and give A to B = 3, C to D = 4 and E to F = 8. The covering A drawn in P4 matches P3, and P4 has a valid 4-flip loop with an impossible 5 or 7. Ribbons follow (the example LRRLR is drawn correctly), then the parity and lower-bound proofs, and two counts of 20. There is more than forty minutes of substantial work, and the proofs give a real challenge. The only edits are labels for the P1 coverings and the footer.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 develops the up/down coloring argument through sharply contrasting boards: the imbalanced hexagon, the balanced but pinched hourglass, the fewest-green bound with proof, chevrons and the converse rule, and every board and answer checks out.
overall.weakest: No band has a mathematical error; the weakest points are small practical gaps: K-1 does not say how children record the coverings in P3 and P6 (which also uses up blue blocks), and P6 in grades 2-3 is ambiguous about pieces that touch only at a corner.
